claim: Temperature is a key driver of transmission of mosquito-borne diseases.
source: Temperature is a key driver of transmission of mosquito-borne diseases.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research establishing this relationship

claim: Both mosquitoes and the pathogens they transmit are ectotherms whose physiology and life histories depend strongly on environmental temperature.
source: Both mosquitoes and the pathogens they transmit are ectotherms whose physiology and life histories depend strongly on environmental temperature (Johnson et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2019; Mordecai et al., 2017; Mordecai et al., 2013; Paull et al., 2017; Rogers and Randolph, 2006; Shocket et al., 2018; Tesla et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies

claim: Mechanistic models based on temperature-dependent traits predict that the thermal response of transmission is unimodal: transmission peaks at intermediate temperatures and declines at extreme cold and hot temperatures.
source: Mechanistic models based on these traits and guided by principles of thermal biology predict that the thermal response of transmission is unimodal: transmission peaks at intermediate temperatures and declines at extreme cold and hot temperatures (Johnson et al., 2015; Liu-Helmersson et al., 2014; Martens et al., 1997; Mordecai et al., 2019; Mordecai et al., 2017; Mordecai et al., 2013; Parham and Michael, 2010; Paull et al., 2017; Shocket et al., 2018; Tesla et al., 2018; Wesolowski et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous modeling studies

claim: This unimodal response is predicted consistently across mosquito-borne diseases.
source: This unimodal response is predicted consistently across mosquito-borne diseases (Johnson et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2019; Mordecai et al., 2017; Mordecai et al., 2013; Paull et al., 2017; Shocket et al., 2018; Tesla et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies

claim: Positive relationships between temperature and human cases have been found in many settings.
source: supported by independent empirical evidence for positive relationships between temperature and human cases in many settings (Stewart-Ibarra and Lowe, 2013; Paull et al., 2017; Peña-García et al., 2017; Siraj et al., 2015; Werner et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies

claim: Negative relationships between temperature and transmission have been found at high temperatures in some studies.
source: but negative relationships at high temperatures in other studies (Gatton et al., 2005; Mordecai et al., 2013; Peña-García et al., 2017; Perkins et al., 2015; Shah et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies

claim: Increasing temperatures due to climate change are expected to shift disease distributions geographically and seasonally, increasing transmission in cooler settings but decreasing it in settings near or above the optimal temperature for transmission.
source: Accordingly, we expect increasing temperatures due to climate change to shift disease distributions geographically and seasonally, as warming increases transmission in cooler settings but decreases it in settings near or above the optimal temperature for transmission (Lafferty, 2009; Lafferty and Mordecai, 2016; Rohr et al., 2011; Ryan et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on the unimodal thermal response and supported by citations

claim: Thermal responses vary among mosquito and pathogen species and drive important differences in how predicted transmission responds to temperature.
source: However, thermal responses vary among mosquito and pathogen species and drive important differences in how predicted transmission responds to temperature, including the specific temperatures of the optimum and thermal limits for each vector–pathogen pair (Johnson et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2019; Mordecai et al., 2017; Mordecai et al., 2013; Paull et al., 2017; Shocket et al., 2018; Tesla et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: West Nile virus is the most common mosquito-borne disease in the US, Canada, and Europe.
source: Since invading North America in 1999, WNV is now distributed worldwide (Kilpatrick, 2011; Rohr et al., 2011) and is the most common mosquito-borne disease in the US, Canada, and Europe.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: SLEV, EEEV, and WEEV occur in the Western hemisphere with cases in North, Central, and South America.
source: SLEV, EEEV, and WEEV occur in the Western hemisphere (Table 1), with cases in North, Central, and South America (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2018a; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2018b; Go et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to CDC and literature sources

claim: North American strains of EEEV are genetically distinct and more virulent than the Central and South American strains.
source: For EEEV, North American strains are genetically distinct and more virulent than the Central and South American strains (Go et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: An unusually large outbreak of EEEV in the United States in 2019 yielded incidence four times higher than average (31 cases, resulting in nine fatalities).
source: An unusually large outbreak of EEEV in the United States in 2019 has yielded incidence four times higher than average (31 cases, resulting in nine fatalities) and brought renewed attention to this disease (Bates, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to a 2019 source

claim: SINV occurs across Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia, with substantial transmission in northern Europe and southern Africa.
source: SINV occurs across Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia, with substantial transmission in northern Europe and southern Africa (Adouchief et al., 2016; Go et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: RVFV originated in eastern Africa and now also occurs across Africa and the Middle East.
source: RVFV originated in eastern Africa and now also occurs across Africa and the Middle East (Linthicum et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: For all six viruses studied, humans are dead-end or unimportant reservoir hosts.
source: For all six viruses, humans are dead-end or unimportant reservoir hosts (Go et al., 2014; Sang et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Most transmission of RVFV to humans occurs through direct contact with infected livestock.
source: Most transmission of RVFV to humans occurs through direct contact with infected livestock (that are infected by mosquitoes), and to a lesser extent via the mosquito-borne transmission from infected vectors (Sang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Cx. pipiens occurs in higher latitude temperate areas in the Northern and Southern hemisphere.
source: Cx. pipiens occurs in higher latitude temperate areas in the Northern and Southern hemisphere, while Cx. quinquefasciatus occurs in lower latitude temperate and tropical areas (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figure 2A showing geographic distributions

claim: Cx. quinquefasciatus occurs in lower latitude temperate and tropical areas.
source: Cx. pipiens occurs in higher latitude temperate areas in the Northern and Southern hemisphere, while Cx. quinquefasciatus occurs in lower latitude temperate and tropical areas (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figure 2A showing geographic distributions

claim: Cx. tarsalis is limited to North America but spans the tropical-temperate gradient.
source: By contrast, Cx. tarsalis is limited to North America but spans the tropical-temperate gradient (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2B showing geographic distribution

claim: All mosquito traits measured were temperature-sensitive.
source: All mosquito traits were temperature-sensitive (three main Culex species: Figure 3, Figure 4; Ae. taeniorhynchus, Ae. triseriatus, Ae. vexans, Cx. theileri, and Cs. melanura: Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: For most species, larval traits (mosquito development rate and survival) produced clear unimodal thermal responses with relatively low uncertainty.
source: For most species, the extensive data for larval traits (mosquito development rate [MDR] and survival [pLA]) produced clear unimodal thermal responses with relatively low uncertainty (Figure 3A,B, Appendix 1—figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: Adult lifespan data decreased linearly over the entire temperature range of available data instead of peaking at intermediate temperatures.
source: However, adult lifespan (lf) data clearly contrasted with expectations from previous studies of more tropical mosquitoes. Lifespan (lf) decreased linearly over the entire temperature range of available data (coldest treatments: 14–16°C, Figure 3D; 22°C, Appendix 1—figure 1D) instead of peaking at intermediate temperatures (e.g. previously published optima for more tropical species: 22.2–23.4°C) (Johnson et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2017; Mordecai et al., 2013; Shocket et al., 2018; Tesla et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures and comparison to previous studies

claim: The thermal responses for pathogen development rate were similar among most vector–virus pairs.
source: The thermal responses for pathogen development rate (PDR) were similar among most vector–virus pairs (Figure 5), with a few notable exceptions
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5

claim: WNV in Cx. quinquefasciatus had a warmer lower thermal limit for pathogen development rate.
source: WNV in Cx. quinquefasciatus had a warmer lower thermal limit (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The thermal response of vector competence and its component traits varied substantially across vectors and viruses.
source: By contrast, the thermal response of vector competence (bc) and its component traits varied substantially across vectors and viruses (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6

claim: Relative R0 responded unimodally to temperature for all the vector–virus pairs, with many peaking at fairly cool temperatures (medians: 22.7–26.0°C).
source: Relative R0 responded unimodally to temperature for all the vector–virus pairs, with many peaking at fairly cool temperatures (medians: 22.7–26.0°C, see Table 2 for CIs; Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 7 and Table 2

claim: The lower thermal limits (medians: 8.7–19.0°C) were more variable than the optima or the upper thermal limits (medians: 31.9–37.8°C).
source: The lower thermal limits (medians: 8.7–19.0°C, see Table 2 for CIs; Figure 7) were more variable than the optima or the upper thermal limits (medians: 31.9–37.8°C, see Table 2 for CIs; Figure 7)
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 7 and Table 2

claim: The upper thermal limit was warmer for WNV transmitted by Cx. pipiens (34.9°C) than by Cx. quinquefasciatus (31.8°C).
source: The upper thermal limit was warmer for WNV transmitted by Cx. pipiens (34.9°C [CI: 32.9–37.5°C]) than by Cx. quinquefasciatus (31.8°C [CI: 31.1–32.2°C])
evidence: Supported by model results with credible intervals

claim: The lower thermal limit for transmission was most often determined by pathogen development rate or biting rate.
source: The lower thermal limit for transmission was most often determined by pathogen development rate (PDR; WNV and SLEV in Cx. tarsalis, WNV in Cx. quinquefasciatus) or biting rate (a; WNV in Cx. univitattus, WEEV in Cx. tarsalis, EEEV in Ae. triseriatus, RVFV and SINV in Ae. taeniorhynchus, SINV in Cx. pipiens; Appendix 1—figures 12–20)
evidence: Supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in appendix figures

claim: The upper thermal limit was determined by biting rate for the three Cx. tarsalis models and by adult lifespan for all others.
source: The upper thermal limit was determined by biting rate (a) for the three Cx. tarsalis models and by adult lifespan (lf) for all others, although proportion ovipositing (pO) was also important for WNV in Cx. quinquefasciatus (Appendix 1—figures 11–20).
evidence: Supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in appendix figures

claim: In all models, lifespan and biting rate had the strongest impact on the optimal temperature for transmission.
source: In all models, lifespan (lf) and biting rate (a) had the strongest impact on the optimal temperature for transmission, with biting rate increasing transmission at low temperatures and lifespan decreasing transmission at high temperatures (Appendix 1—figures 11–20).
evidence: Supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in appendix figures

claim: Incidence of human neuroinvasive West Nile disease responded unimodally to average summer temperature and peaked at 24°C.
source: Incidence of human neuroinvasive West Nile disease responded unimodally to average summer temperature and peaked at 24°C (23.5–24.2°C depending on the spline settings; Figure 8, Appendix 1—figure 24)
evidence: Supported by GAM analysis of county-level human case data shown in Figure 8

claim: The optimal temperature for human WNV cases (24°C) closely matched the optima from the mechanistic models for the three North American Culex species (23.9–25.2°C).
source: peaked at 24°C (23.5–24.2°C depending on the spline settings; Figure 8, Appendix 1—figure 24), closely matching the optima from the mechanistic models for the three North American Culex species (23.9–25.2°C; Table 2).
evidence: Comparison between empirical case data and model predictions

claim: The human disease data did not show evidence for lower or upper thermal limits.
source: However, the human disease data did not show evidence for lower or upper thermal limits: mean incidence remained positive and with relatively flat slopes below ~19°C and above ~28°C, although sample size was very low above 28°C and below 15°C resulting in wide confidence intervals (Figure 8, Appendix 1—figure 24).
evidence: Supported by analysis of human case data shown in Figure 8

claim: There was a 2-month lag between initial increases in R0 and incidence of WNV cases.
source: As expected (based on previous studies and the time required for mosquito populations to increase, become infectious, and bite humans, and for humans to present symptoms and seek medical care [Mordecai et al., 2017; Shocket et al., 2018]), there was a 2-month lag between initial increases in R0(T) and incidence: cases began rising in June to the peak in August.
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions to month-of-onset data and citations to previous studies

claim: The monotonically decreasing thermal responses of lifespan for these more temperate mosquitoes contrast with the clearly unimodal responses of more tropical species.
source: The monotonically decreasing thermal responses of lifespan (lf) within the range of the available experimental data for these more temperate mosquitoes (Figure 3D) contrast with the clearly unimodal responses of more tropical species (Mordecai et al., 2019; Mordecai et al., 2017; Mordecai et al., 2013; Shocket et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison of data from this study to previous studies

claim: Both Cx. pipiens and Cx. tarsalis diapause.
source: Both Cx. pipiens and Cx. tarsalis diapause (Nelms et al., 2013; Vinogradova, 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Cx. pipiens can survive temperatures at or near freezing (0°C) for several months.
source: Cx. pipiens can survive temperatures at or near freezing (0°C) for several months (Vinogradova, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Cx. quinquefasciatus enters a non-diapause quiescent state.
source: Cx. quinquefasciatus enters a non-diapause quiescent state (Diniz et al., 2017; Nelms et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Predicted transmission for many of the diseases in this study peaked at and extended to cooler temperatures than for previously studied diseases with more tropical distributions.
source: Predicted transmission for many of the diseases in this study peaked at and extended to cooler temperatures than for previously studied diseases with more tropical distributions (see Figure 7 and Table 2 for 95% credible intervals)(Mordecai et al., 2019).
evidence: Comparison of model results to previous studies

claim: The optimal temperatures for transmission varied from 22.7–25.2°C (excluding Ae. taeniorhynchus models).
source: Here, the optimal temperatures for transmission varied from 22.7–25.2°C (excluding Ae. taeniorhynchus models, Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 7

claim: Models predict that transmission of malaria peaks at 25.4°C.
source: By contrast, models predict that transmission peaks at 25.4°C for malaria (Johnson et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous modeling studies

claim: Models predict that transmission of Ross River virus peaks at 26.4°C.
source: 26.4°C for Ross River virus (Shocket et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous modeling study

claim: Models predict that transmission of dengue in Ae. albopictus peaks at 26.4°C.
source: 26.4°C for Ross River virus (Shocket et al., 2018) and dengue in Ae. albopictus (Mordecai et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous modeling study

claim: Models predict that transmission of Zika in Ae. aegypti peaks at 28.9°C.
source: 28.9°C for Zika in Ae. aegypti (Tesla et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous modeling study

claim: Models predict that transmission of dengue in Ae. aegypti peaks at 29.1°C.
source: 29.1°C for dengue in Ae. aegypti (Mordecai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous modeling study

claim: Models for several vector–virus pairs had cooler lower thermal limits (medians: 8.7–19.0°C) than those of diseases with more tropical distributions (medians: 16.0–17.8°C).
source: Models for several vector–virus pairs also had cooler lower thermal limits (medians: 8.7–19.0°C) than those of diseases with more tropical distributions (medians: 16.0–17.8°C)(Mordecai et al., 2019).
evidence: Comparison of model results to previous studies

claim: These patterns led to wider thermal breadths (18.2–27.7°C) for most of the viruses here compared to the more tropical pathogens (11.7–16.7°C).
source: In combination with similar upper thermal limits (see below), these patterns led to wider thermal breadths (18.2–27.7°C; Figure 7) for most of the viruses here compared to the more tropical pathogens (11.7–16.7°C), excepting WNV in Cx. quinquefasciatus (12.7°C)
evidence: Comparison of model results to previous studies

claim: These results match a previous finding that temperate insects had wider thermal breadths than tropical insects.
source: These results match a previous finding that temperate insects had wider thermal breadths than tropical insects (Deutsch et al., 2008)
evidence: Comparison to previous study

claim: SINV had the second coolest lower thermal limit.
source: Additionally, SINV—a virus with substantial transmission at very high latitudes in Finland (Adouchief et al., 2016)—had the second coolest lower thermal limit (Figure 7, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 7 and Table 2

claim: Lower latitude Cx. quinquefasciatus outperformed higher latitude Cx. pipiens at warmer temperatures for proportion ovipositing.
source: Further, lower latitude Cx. quinquefasciatus outperformed higher latitude Cx. pipiens at warmer temperatures for proportion ovipositing (pO; Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Higher latitude Cx. pipiens outperformed lower latitude Cx. quinquefasciatus at cooler temperatures for egg viability.
source: while the reverse occurred at cooler temperatures for egg viability (EV; Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Measurements of physiological traits can predict geographic patterns of vectors or disease transmission at broad scales to some extent.
source: Collectively, these results imply that, to some extent, measurements of physiological traits can predict geographic patterns of vectors or disease transmission at broad scales.
evidence: Inference based on the patterns observed in the data

claim: Geographic range differences did not consistently predict variation in thermal responses among the Culex species in this study.
source: However, geographic range differences (Figure 2) did not consistently predict variation in thermal responses among the Culex species in this study (e.g. biting rate [a, Figure 3C] and adult lifespan [lf, Figure 3D])
evidence: Supported by comparison of data to geographic ranges

claim: The upper thermal limits for the vector–virus pairs in this study (31.9–34.9°C, excluding Ae. taeniorhynchus models) closely matched those of more tropical diseases (31.5–34.7°C).
source: In contrast to the optima, lower thermal limits, and thermal breadths, the upper thermal limits for the vector–virus pairs in this study (31.9–34.9°C, excluding Ae. taeniorhynchus models; Figure 7D, Table 2) closely matched those of more tropical diseases (31.5–34.7°C) (Johnson et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2017; Mordecai et al., 2013; Shocket et al., 2018; Tesla et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison of model results to previous studies

claim: Maximum summer temperatures in temperate areas can match or even exceed maximum temperatures in tropical areas.
source: This similarity may arise because maximum summer temperatures in temperate areas can match or even exceed maximum temperatures in tropical areas (Sunday et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: There may be a fundamental upper thermal constraint on transmission that applies similarly to all mosquito-borne diseases, driven by short mosquito lifespans at high temperatures.
source: Accordingly, there may be a fundamental upper thermal constraint on transmission that applies similarly to all mosquito-borne diseases, driven by short mosquito lifespans at high temperatures.
evidence: Inference based on the similarity of upper thermal limits across diseases

claim: As temperatures rise due to climate change, temperate diseases are unlikely to be displaced by warming alone.
source: These results indicate that as temperatures rise due to climate change, temperate diseases are unlikely to be displaced by warming alone, although they may also expand toward the poles, even as tropical diseases may expand farther into temperate zones.
evidence: Inference based on the model results showing similar upper thermal limits

claim: Human cases of WNV are often positively associated with temperature.
source: Human cases of WNV (Ahmadnejad et al., 2016; Hahn et al., 2015; Marcantonio et al., 2015; Platonov et al., 2008; Reisen et al., 2006; Semenza et al., 2016; Shand et al., 2016) and SINV (Brummer-Korvenkontio et al., 2002; Jalava et al., 2013) are often positively associated with temperature.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies

claim: Human cases of SINV are often positively associated with temperature.
source: Human cases of WNV (Ahmadnejad et al., 2016; Hahn et al., 2015; Marcantonio et al., 2015; Platonov et al., 2008; Reisen et al., 2006; Semenza et al., 2016; Shand et al., 2016) and SINV (Brummer-Korvenkontio et al., 2002; Jalava et al., 2013) are often positively associated with temperature.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Temperature variation over time may sustain transmission in regions with otherwise unsuitable mean summer temperatures by providing time windows that are suitable for transmission.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that temperature variation over time may sustain transmission in regions with otherwise unsuitable mean summer temperatures by providing time windows that are suitable for transmission.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed to explain the lack of observed thermal limits in field data

claim: The 2-month lag between climate suitability and the onset of human cases matches previous results from other mosquito-borne diseases.
source: The 2-month lag between climate suitability and the onset of human cases, which matches previous results from other mosquito-borne diseases (Mordecai et al., 2017; Shocket et al., 2018)
evidence: Comparison to previous studies

claim: Both Cx. pipiens and Cx. tarsalis shift their feeding preferences from birds to humans as wild birds begin to migrate in late summer.
source: Additionally, as wild birds begin to migrate in late summer, both Cx. pipiens and Cx. tarsalis shift their feeding preferences from birds to humans, which should increase transmission to people later in the year (Kilpatrick et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Drought, precipitation, and reservoir and human immunity strongly drive transmission of WNV.
source: Drought, precipitation, and reservoir and human immunity also strongly drive transmission of WNV (Ahmadnejad et al., 2016; Marcantonio et al., 2015; Paull et al., 2017; Shand et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Transmission of WEEV is favored over SLEV in cooler conditions.
source: SLEV, EEEV, and WEEV are less common in nature, and thus less well-studied, but the lower thermal limits in our study support previous findings that transmission of WEEV is favored over SLEV in cooler conditions (Hess et al., 1963).
evidence: Model results support previous findings cited

claim: Mean temperature is not associated with outbreaks of RVFV.
source: By contrast, mean temperature is not associated with outbreaks of RVFV, although they are highly predictable based on precipitation driven by El Niño–Southern Oscillation cycles (Anyamba et al., 2009; Linthicum et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Two previous models predicted that transmission of WNV would increase up to the warmest temperatures they considered, 28°C and 35°C.
source: Two previous models predicted that transmission of WNV would increase up to the warmest temperatures they considered, 28°C (Vogels et al., 2017) and 35°C (Kushmaro et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison to previous modeling studies

claim: A previous study with models for Cx. pipiens, Cx. quiquefasciatus, and Cx. tarsalis predicted unimodal thermal responses for transmission, with very similar optima but with lower thermal limits that were ~5°C warmer, resulting in much narrower thermal breadths.
source: A third study with models for Cx. pipiens, Cx. quiquefasciatus, and Cx. tarsalis, like our study, predicted unimodal thermal responses for transmission, with very similar optima but with lower thermal limits that were ~5°C warmer, resulting in much narrower thermal breadths (Appendix 1—figure 23; Paull et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison to previous modeling study

claim: Currently the majority of people (70%) and counties (68%) in the US are below the optimal temperature for WNV transmission (23.9°C).
source: Based on the average summer temperature data (2001–2016) in our analysis (Figure 8), currently the majority of people (70%) and counties (68%) are below the optimal temperature for transmission (23.9°C, fit by the GAM).
evidence: Analysis of temperature data relative to model predictions

claim: We might expect a net increase in transmission of West Nile virus in response to the warming climate, even as hot temperatures suppress transmission in some places.
source: Thus, all else being equal, we might expect a net increase in transmission of West Nile virus in response to the warming climate, even as hot temperatures suppress transmission in some places.
evidence: Inference based on the proportion of locations below optimal temperature

claim: Warming is unlikely to eliminate any of these more temperate pathogens since the upper thermal limits for transmission are well above temperatures pathogens regularly experience in their current geographic ranges.
source: Still, warming is unlikely to eliminate any of these more temperate pathogens since the upper thermal limits for transmission are well above temperatures pathogens regularly experience in their current geographic ranges.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of upper thermal limits to current temperatures

claim: Transmission of West Nile virus peaks at temperatures between 23°C and 26°C.
source: Transmission of West Nile and five other temperate mosquito-borne viruses peaks at temperatures between 23°C and 26°C
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the title and supported by model results

claim: The incidence of human West Nile virus cases across US counties responded unimodally to average summer temperature and peaked at 24°C, matching model-predicted optima (24–25°C).
source: The incidence of human West Nile virus cases across US counties responded unimodally to average summer temperature and peaked at 24°C, matching model-predicted optima (24–25°C).
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by analysis of human case data

claim: Climate warming will likely shift transmission of these diseases, increasing it in cooler locations while decreasing it in warmer locations.
source: Climate warming will likely shift transmission of these diseases, increasing it in cooler locations while decreasing it in warmer locations.
evidence: Prediction stated in abstract based on unimodal thermal response

claim: West Nile virus has caused 7 million estimated infections, 22,999 neuroinvasive cases, and 2163 deaths in the US since invading in 1999.
source: Since invading in 1999, 7 million estimated infections, 22,999 neuroinvasive cases, and 2163 deaths in US
evidence: Epidemiological data from Table 1

claim: West Nile virus has caused 5614 reported cases in Canada.
source: 5614 reported cases in Canada.
evidence: Epidemiological data from Table 1

claim: There are typically 100–300 cases of West Nile virus annually in Europe, but over 1500 in 2018.
source: Typically 100–300 cases annually in Europe, but over 1500 in 2018.
evidence: Epidemiological data from Table 1

claim: Seroprevalence of West Nile virus is approximately 80% in some areas of Africa.
source: Poor surveillance in Africa, but seroprevalence ~ 80% in some areas.
evidence: Epidemiological data from Table 1

claim: Birds are the main reservoir/amplification hosts for West Nile virus.
source: Birds are main reservoir/amplification hosts.
evidence: Ecological information from Table 1

claim: St. Louis Encephalitis virus has 5–15% mortality in diagnosed cases.
source: Encephalitis. 5–15% mortality in diagnosed cases.
evidence: Clinical data from Table 1

claim: 92 cases and six deaths of St. Louis Encephalitis virus were recorded in the US from 2009 to 2018.
source: 92 cases and six deaths recorded in US from 2009 to 2018.
evidence: Epidemiological data from Table 1

claim: Eastern Equine Encephalitis virus has 33% mortality in diagnosed cases.
source: Febrile illness and encephalitis. 33% mortality in diagnosed cases.
evidence: Clinical data from Table 1

claim: 73 cases and 30 deaths of Eastern Equine Encephalitis virus were recorded in the US from 2009 to 2018.
source: 73 cases and 30 deaths recorded in US from 2009 to 2018.
evidence: Epidemiological data from Table 1

claim: 640 cases of Western Equine Encephalitis virus were recorded in the US from 1964 to 2010.
source: 640 cases recorded in US from 1964 to 2010.
evidence: Epidemiological data from Table 1

claim: WEEV is derived from a recombinant event between the ancestors of EEEV and SINV.
source: WEEV is derived from a recombinant event between the ancestors of EEEV and SINV.
evidence: Evolutionary information from Table 1

claim: Annual incidence of Sindbis virus in Finland is 2–26 per 100,000 people.
source: Poor surveillance except in Finland, where annual incidence is 2–26 per 100,000 people
evidence: Epidemiological data from Table 1

claim: Seroprevalence of Sindbis virus can reach approximately 40% in Finland.
source: seroprevalence can reach ~40%
evidence: Epidemiological data from Table 1

claim: Long-distance migratory birds may spread Sindbis virus between temperate zones in Northern and Southern hemispheres.
source: Long-distance migratory birds may spread the virus between temperate zones in Northern and Southern hemispheres.
evidence: Ecological hypothesis from Table 1

claim: Rift Valley Fever virus has less than 1% mortality in total cases.
source: Febrile illness and encephalitis. < 1% mortality in total cases.
evidence: Clinical data from Table 1

claim: Rift Valley Fever virus has 50% mortality in hemorrhagic cases.
source: 50% mortality in hemorrhagic cases
evidence: Clinical data from Table 1

claim: Rift Valley Fever virus causes permanent blindness in 50% of ocular cases.
source: permanent blindness in 50% of ocular cases (<2% of cases)
evidence: Clinical data from Table 1

claim: Livestock are the main reservoir/amplification hosts for Rift Valley Fever virus.
source: Livestock are main reservoir/amplification hosts, and suffer mortality and abortion after being infected by mosquitoes.
evidence: Ecological information from Table 1

claim: Vertical transmission in vectors via dormant eggs can initiate epidemics of Rift Valley Fever virus.
source: Vertical transmission in vectors (via dormant eggs) can initiate epidemics.
evidence: Ecological information from Table 1

claim: In eastern and southern Africa, there are large epidemics of Rift Valley Fever virus every 5–15 years driven by rainfall and blooms of Aedes species.
source: In eastern and southern Africa, there are large epidemics every 5–15 years driven by rainfall and blooms of Ae. spp. from low-lying flooded areas known as dambos.
evidence: Epidemiological pattern from Table 1
